To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
long LOD was associated with more negative patient-reported outcomes, and was a significant predictor of work outcomes at 12 months after treatment discharge.
longer LOD was a risk for program non-completion, was associated with worse patient-reported outcomes at admission and was a significant predictor of work outcomes at 12 months post-treatment.

longer disability was associated with more pain, depression and disability at admission, and with less likelihood of returning to work and retaining work after treatment, but still, a high percentage of patients with long LOD did return to work after treatment, which suggests that the FRP is an effective intervention for these patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of extended disability duration on the effectiveness of FRP treatment for chronic occupational MSD.

the effects of extended length of disability (beyond 24 months) on the outcomes of a functional restoration program (FRP) for patients with chronic, disabling occupational musculoskeletel disorders (CDOMD).
the effects of extended disability duration on treatment outcomes in a large FRP patient cohort, and the implications of our findings on the design of future FRP research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
extended LOD does have a negative influence on treatment outcomes.
the length of disability is not a barrier to successful treatment outcome in FRPs.
extended LOD (b beyond 18 months) was not a significant barrier to treatment success for FRP patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for CDOMDs patients with LOD longer than 24 months, the odds of returning to work and maintaining work were significantly lower, compared to patients with shorter LOD (≤24 months).

the longer the disability duration between injury and treatment, the more difficult it would be for patients to complete the FRP, and for those who do complete the program, the less likely they are to work.
, although long LOD may be a significant predictor of work outcomes, it does not preclude patients from returning to work.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FRP is an effective treatment for CDOMD patients, regardless of the length of disability.
patients with extended LOD can still benefit from an FRP, even if they have had their disability for 2 or 3 years.
patients with extended LOD (>24 months), who complete an FRP, have a good likelihood to work again.
